stories.headline: Can Jimmy Butler return in time to resurrect Steph Curry's final chapter?
stories.summary: After a quiet offseason, the Warriors know Jimmy Butler's return is their best hope of reaching the playoffs.
stories.body:
IN THE EIGHT months since Jimmy Butler's right knee buckled during the hottest streak of his 15th NBA season, his mood and memory of the traumatic moment have improved as his leg has slowly healed.

He remembers the high-arcing pass from Brandin Podziemski while rolling toward the rim, the instant he felt Miami Heat guard Davion Mitchell slide under him on the catch and that shooting pain on the landing that incited an arena-silencing scream.

In a conversation with ESPN following the Warriors' third training camp practice, Butler relived the scene. From a padded seat on the sideline, he pointed toward the left block of their temporary practice court in Hawaii. That's where -- face down in the hardwood, eyes closed, letting out a few painful howls -- he can still hear Buddy Hield's distinctive voice off in the distance.

"Get up, Jimmy! Get up! We need you!"

Even in the darkest of split seconds, Butler beamed about his three-word retort to a former teammate he loved to torment: "No s---, Buddy."

Then, Butler rolled over onto his back as everyone began to circle.

"When I opened my eyes, I swear to you," Butler said, raising his hands toward the roof. "It was like Jesus was standing over me."

Butler is referring to Stephen Curry. Butler locked eyes with his star teammate, whom Butler calls Batman, and noticed an unnerved look on Curry's face. Curry knew.

"He's super tough," Curry told ESPN. "He's not very dramatic when it comes to stuff like that. He usually plays it off. Him and Buddy started talking trash to each other, and in that moment, I knew he was trying to kind of cope."

After a wobbly 13-15 start to the regular season, the Warriors were 11-4 in the 15-game stretch before Butler's ACL injury vs. Miami, coinciding with a ferocious stretch of productivity from Butler, who averaged 21 points, five rebounds and five assists.

In his last game before the injury, Butler went for 32 points on 14-of-22 shooting in a blowout over the eventual champion New York Knicks. The Warriors' record had spiked back to a reasonable 25-19.

"We knew we were still good," Warriors coach Steve Kerr told ESPN. "And we knew as long as we were healthy, we were dangerous and we'd make some noise. But Jimmy goes down, and instantly you just know deep down your championship aspirations are gone."

Butler's injury occurred more than two weeks before the trade deadline. To acquire Giannis Antetokounmpo, the Warriors would've needed to trade either Butler's or Draymond Green's contract, had the Milwaukee Bucks desired Golden State's pick package, which included its four available first-rounders. But the Bucks balked, and Butler has never been offered in other potential trades, team sources said.

Though the market views an injured Butler as a negative value on an expiring $56.8 million deal, general manager Mike Dunleavy still sees him as an essential part of the next few years. A large part of Dunleavy's offseason inactivity is rooted in his belief that Butler is a major ingredient toward winning, with impactful days still ahead.

The Warriors didn't show an appetite to offer Butler for Anthony Davis or Jaylen Brown this summer, considering the pick packages required and contracts attached to both. All other Butler-plus-picks conversations -- for what the Warriors believe are ultimately lesser players once Butler returns -- were shut down, team sources said.

That unwillingness to move Butler has put the Warriors in a perceived purgatory to open the season. They are an afterthought, missing $69 million in starting wings (Butler and the injured Moses Moody) and predicted by most as a lottery-bound team in the bottom third of the Western Conference.

But almost every bigger-picture conversation with those in the organization almost immediately shifts to Butler, who just turned 37, and the perhaps unfair burden he might face to rescue their hopes in his first few months back from ACL rehab.

"I'm almost looking at this like this could be the exact opposite of last season," Kerr said. "We get Jimmy back around February instead of losing him in February. So, what's our job? Lay the best foundation, best platform for success before that, that can put us in a good position where we've got momentum, and all of a sudden, we're adding him with the playoffs coming a couple months later. I think the plan is there."

CURRY WAS AMONG a large contingent within the Warriors initially skeptical of acquiring Butler after his elongated final chapter in Miami played out like a soap opera.

They had discussed Zach LaVine as an alternative option, team sources said. Curry was also fond of Andrew Wiggins, a beloved teammate who helped push Curry to that legacy-cementing fourth title in 2022 but would need to be moved to make a deal work. So Curry, while informed, stayed mostly out of front office business, as he prefers.

Dunleavy pushed hardest for the Butler trade, convincing Warriors owner Joe Lacob and the necessary power players of it before delivering a two-year, $111 million extension to satisfy Butler and muscle it across the finish line.

Dunleavy, a 15-year pro, played with Butler in Chicago for three seasons. Dunleavy was around when Butler declined a four-year, $44 million max extension before his fourth season, and Butler has said Dunleavy was one of the Bulls' veterans who convinced him early he was on a star trajectory.

"Then, he just blew up," Dunleavy said. "Unquestioned max. That was fun to watch as a teammate."

Dunleavy was confident that Butler would appreciate Kerr, Curry, the winning atmosphere and the relaxed climate both have cultivated. Dunleavy figured Butler would vibe with Green off the court and click on the defensive end. Dunleavy assumed that Butler's toughness, approach and superior ability would win over everyone.

Dunleavy proved correct. Butler debuted in Chicago for a middling Warriors team (25-25 record) and already had Kerr, Curry and Green beaming about him postgame, calling his turnover-averse, interior-focused, free-throw-heavy style a perfect complement to Curry's and Butler's attitude and exactly the jolt a flat season needed.

"He's a lion," Kerr called him.

The Warriors sprinted to a 23-8 finish with Butler, upset the Houston Rockets in the first round and still internally believe they could've and probably would've eliminated the Minnesota Timberwolves in the second round had Curry not injured his hamstring.

That bred an unwavering confidence in the Warriors' championship viability last season until Butler tore his ACL.

"He's such an alpha," Kerr said. "Everyone feels so confident when he's on the floor. He's also a total wiseass. The humor, the dynamic that exists with him in the locker room. There's just a sense of swagger that you have when Jimmy's on your team. So, it felt like we lost that instantly."

The rest of the season was a slow nightmare. Curry was sidelined for two months to tend to a persistent knee issue. They traded for Kristaps Porzingis, who was in and out of the lineup. They went 12-26 after the Butler injury, fading to the background in a season that opened with quiet title belief.

"I really felt like I let Steph down," Butler said. "I let Draymond down. I let Steve down. Because they took a chance. If you don't know me and you haven't been around me, you don't know what I'm about because of the things that you may read and hear. But they said, 'F--- all of that s---. This motherf---er knows how to win.' They took a chance, and I felt I let them down."

MOODY RUPTURED HIS left patellar tendon in late March, a frightening injury that required a stretcher to get him off the floor, further debilitating the supporting cast in the fading seasons of the Curry era.

But Moody has since described it as a "best-case scenario" rupture. Doctors told him it was a clean tear from the bone instead of a rupture in the middle of the tendon, which should simplify and quicken his rehab.

The recovery results have been encouraging. Team sources indicate that Moody is ahead of Butler's pace, and the internal expectation is that Moody will return before Butler.

Neither has advanced beyond individual court work, and there are several checkpoints to hit, but the current belief is Moody could return in the December-to-January range, and Butler could be back in the January-to-February range. Butler said the next step in his rehab is landing from a game speed-type jump without issue or concern.

"I know [an exact target date]," Butler said with a smile. "We know. Y'all just find out whenever y'all find out."

Much of Dunleavy's roster planning during the past couple of years has been about flexibility and optionality. The Warriors are loaded with expiring contracts and capable of clearing up to nearly $60 million in cap space next summer.

"These [semi-rebuild] processes are painful," Kerr said. "They take a few years. Mike has been brilliant just sort of guiding us to this point, and next summer, all of a sudden for the first time in forever, we'll have all this cap space and these young players we like. We can see the other side now."

Butler -- like Green, a franchise legend -- is among the incumbent players who hope and believe portions of that cap space will be used to retain them. Butler has continually stated his desire to retire with the Warriors.

That dynamic will loom in the background around the time Butler is prepping for the final stages of his return, having a limited amount of runway to reinvigorate his value before hitting free agency. He becomes extension-eligible Feb. 6.

"I don't pay attention to it," Butler said. "My job is to go out there and hoop. You got to talk to [my agent] Bernie Lee, you got to talk to Mike Dunleavy, whoever else specializes in that aspect. My job is to help us win, to compete at a high level and be the best leader, teammate, vet that I can to these young guys. That's what I control. So, that's what I do control."

DUNLEAVY FINALIZED THE trade for Butler on the same night the Warriors were playing the Jazz in Utah. It was a somber, tear-filled pregame locker room as the team said goodbye to Wiggins and three other teammates.

After the game, Green and Curry said they started to envision the future with Butler and what the trade meant. Green has said Curry told him that night: "This is it. This is our last ride."

There was always a belief that the Butler trade was the final big-ticket lever the front office was pulling in the Curry chapter, costing only a first-round pick as management also protected its future.

It's possible that Butler's ACL tear abruptly ended that chapter and any realistic chance at contention. But Butler has now crept past the eight-month mark since his ACL surgery, and Curry, ever the optimist, said he believes the dream of that final chapter with Butler has a chance at resurrection.

"I can," Curry said. "Just like the same way he got here 2½ years ago [and changed everything]. Nobody predicted that. And I know he loves it here. I know this is a place he felt at home. Every day is information for us as a team and organization. And I know he understands that, but everything that we're doing and everything we said over the summer is to hold the fort down until he gets back. That's our job as players. So we're on that mission."

While Curry was going through his own tricky knee rehab last March, he visited Butler in Los Angeles, and the two bonded during a low point in the later stages of their careers, further motivating Butler to change the narrative of this closing chapter.

"I just want to help those guys win another [title], man," Butler said. "And get me one. I felt I let them down. Now, as I'm going through this rehab process, as I'm starting to move and run and jump, I'm like, oh s---, I could still do it. And that's why I say y'all motherf---ers going to be real shocked if y'all think I'm going to come back and be some bum a-- player."

What does he think about those who doubt he can return anywhere near his former self and that his aging Warriors have no chance to contend?

"I don't give a f---, honestly," Butler said. "I bet y'all not going to leave me. I bet no team going to be like, 'Oh, no, don't guard that guy.' They're not going to do that. I bet whenever I step on the floor, they're going to send more than one body. I bet you're still going to foul me. So what are we talking about here?"

stories.headline: DraftKings DFS cheat sheet: Best values for Sunday's main slate
stories.summary: Build a winning DFS lineup with our DraftKings NFL Week 6 cheat sheet identifying the best stacks and values
stories.body:
Set a winning lineup for DraftKings' NFL Sunday main slate by combining value picks in each roster slot and exploiting the best matchups, all within the confines of the salary cap. Every week, we evaluate all of your DraftKings options to identify the best values among the lower-priced options, as well as the matchups to play or avoid, so you can select the players who are worth their high price tags.

Value is determined by the number of DraftKings points you can expect for every dollar invested in putting that player in your lineup. A player might be an "average" or even a "good" value while also projected to outscore a player identified as a "great value," but when you consider the cap hit and the salary you can put toward other players, you might decide that the "great" value outweighs that projection.

Players considered to be a "great" value are those in the 90th percentile of projected value picks for the week. "Good" plays are in the 75th percentile or better. "Average" plays span the 25th to 74th percentiles, and "shaky" plays are in the 10th-24th percentiles. "Poor" picks encompass single-digit percentiles. Only players projected to score 4 points or more are displayed.

Player salaries are drawn from DraftKings' main slate and are based on the ESPN player projections at the time of publication.

stories.summary: Just a pair of showdowns for hockey fans to watch on Friday -- but they're both superb. Here's what you need to know.
stories.body:
For there to be 16 games on the NHL schedule on Tuesday, then 11 on Thursday and 14 on Saturday, there must also be days with fewer games.

Friday is such a day, as there are only two games on the docket. On the plus side, they are both superb matchups, featuring interconference matchups between four teams that made the 2026 Stanley Cup playoffs.

Here's a look at the key stats and storylines for each, along with betting info and broadcast details:

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

Pittsburgh Penguins at Colorado Avalanche

9 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | COL -218, O/U: 6.5

Although the Penguins and Avs are not traditional rivals, their matchups will always be fun to watch as long as Sidney Crosby and Nathan MacKinnon are facing off against each other. The Cole Harbour, Nova Scotia natives are future Hall of Famers and friends ... and also two of the most passionate competitors in the NHL. The teams traded blowout wins last season (a 7-2 Penguins win on March 16 and a 6-2 Avs win on March 24). Hopefully that trend of high-scoring games continues in this one. (Sorry, goalies.)

Boston Bruins at Anaheim Ducks

10 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | BOS -120, O/U: 6.5

The Bruins are one game into their California swing, and left San Jose with a 6-3 win. Can the Ducks offer a tougher challenge? For those interested in the next generation of superstars, this game features a handful of them, including Anaheim's Leo Carlsson, Cutter Gauthier, Beckett Sennecke and Jackson LaCombe, along with Boston's Fraser Minten and James Hagens.

stories.headline: Man City's alternate universe: Guardiola, Haaland to Arsenal? Arteta to PSG?
stories.summary: The course of soccer history could be very different for a lot of players and teams if Man City had stayed within the rules, so what could have happened?
stories.body:
On Sept. 1, 2008, the course of Premier League history changed. Manchester City were bought by the Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), led by Sheikh Mansour -- an Emirati royal, the vice president of the United Arab Emirates, and one of the richest men in the world -- for around £200 million.

What followed over the next 18 years was a flood of cash -- including over £3 billion spent on transfers -- that propelled City to the top of the sport, allowing them to sign 123 players and sweep up trophy after trophy. Under ADUG ownership, the club has won 26 of them: eight Premier League titles, four FA Cups, seven Carabao Cups, four Community Shields, a UEFA Champions League, a Club World Cup and a Super Cup.

But in September 2026, an independent commission ruled that the club was guilty of 114 charges in relation to breaches of the Premier League's spending rules, while artificially inflating its sponsorship figures by more than £830 million in a nine-year period between 2009-18. City maintain their innocence and have appealed the decision, but potential sanctions are being scoped out and could include expulsion from the league, a massive points deduction, or relegation.

It begs the question: What would the sport have looked like if City had not spent in the way that they did? Who would have won the eight league titles? Where would the superstars (like Erling Haaland) they signed have gone instead? And what would manager Pep Guardiola's career have looked like without a decade-long stint in Manchester?

Here, we paint an alternate reality where City -- still owned and backed by Sheikh Mansour -- spent modestly (within the rules), never won the 2012 league title, never signed Haaland, and never appointed Guardiola. Much like a Marvel movie set across the multiverse, we can speculate as to what might have transpired in this timeline.

New Premier League winners are crowned

What actually happened: The 2011 FA Cup success started a flood of league trophies as City won titles in 2011-12 (on goal difference), 2013-14 (on the final day of the season), 2017-18 (with a record 100 points and 19-point margin), 2018-19 (by a single point), 2020-21 (during a COVID-impacted season), 2021-22 (on the final day), 2022-23 (as part of treble including FA Cup and Champions League), and 2023-24 (the first club to win four consecutive English top-flight titles.)

Alternate reality: In this timeline, City experience a much more mundane life. They don't spend lavishly, they don't destabilize their closest competitors by continually signing their players, so they don't make the definitive leap to stardom. On the plus side, they also don't fall into financial ruin ... which was a genuine threat before the Abu Dhabi takeover.

No titles for City: 2011-18

One of the Premier League's most iconic moments never happens. Sky Sports commentator Martin Tyler never screams this famous "Agüeroooooooo!" line when Sergio Agüero scores a 94th-minute winner against QPR to win the 2011-12 title, because Agüero never joins City for £35 million in 2011. Here, City can't use the preceding three years to spend hundreds of millions and assemble a title-winning team.

Instead, Manchester United win the 2011-12 Premier League, rather than losing it on goal difference with 89 points, and Sir Alex Ferguson's title count ends at 14 -- not 13 -- when he retires after winning another the following season. In 2013-14, Liverpool secure the title, not City, as Steven Gerrard's slip against Chelsea makes no difference. Brendan Rodgers wins the Premier League, but the club still hires Jürgen Klopp in 2015, as Rodgers simply gets a bit more time before imploding and the German arrives.

Chelsea sign several players (we'll cover them in more detail later) who would have ended up at City -- the likes of David Silva and Kyle Walker -- so their two titles in the next three years under Jose Mourinho and then Antonio Conte, as well as the incredible 2015-16 title run of Leicester City (this multiverse is not cruel), remain unchanged.

And what of City's centurion season in 2017-18? That 100-point haul stands as a Premier League record and was sealed in the most dramatic of circumstances, with Gabriel Jesus scoring at the death on the final day to beat Southampton, but the team that achieved it was not compiled in this timeline, so it goes to Manchester United instead and Mourinho gets himself another medal.

That brings us to the end of the period during which City have been charged. However, without the successes between 2009-18, the club has no empire to continue to dominate from, so it changes the face of the next seven years too.

The next seven years: 2019-26

Klopp's Liverpool win back-to-back titles in 2018-19 and 2019-20 -- the one they actually won -- and claim another in 2021-22.

In the middle of that, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer leads Manchester United to a title, which changes the very nature of how he is perceived as a coach -- though it's fair to assume that the club's struggles to replace the legendary Ferguson continue in the same vein, albeit with a few more titles, and he doesn't last much longer.

Arsenal get in on the act, too. Their torturous 2022-23 and 2023-24 seasons, in which they were narrowly beaten to the title by City twice, take on a very different inflection as they canter to victory and set up a dynasty of their own. (Stay tuned for who their manager is from 2021 onwards.)

But if one thing has been proven in every multiverse, it's that no matter how much money Chelsea spend on megastars, nothing can make them consistent. In this timeline, they'll win a handful of cups and challenge much more strongly for the league, but the revolving door of managers means their star players never truly settle and drive them to another title after 2016-17.

City's rivals grow stronger

What happened: Manchester City's strategy to accelerate into the elite was to spend big in a relatively methodical way early on, but the key was to sign their competitors' star players.

From Arsenal, they took Emmanuel Adebayor (£25 million) and Kolo Touré (£16 million) in 2009, Samir Nasri (£24 million) and Gaël Clichy (£10 million) in 2011, and Bacary Sagna (free) in 2014. From Everton they took Joleon Lescott (£22 million) in 2009, Jack Rodwell (£12 million) in 2012 and John Stones (£47.5 million) in 2016. From Aston Villa, they took Gareth Barry (£12 million) in 2009, James Milner (£18 million, plus Stephen Ireland) in 2010, and Fabian Delph (£8 million) in 2015.

But there was another, really big one that sent shockwaves through Manchester and beyond. City brought in Argentina striker Carlos Tevez from West Ham United for £25.5 million on a weekly wage exceeding £200,000 per week -- for context, this was huge in 2009 -- and in the process took him away from Manchester United, who had signed him on loan for two years and had every intention of completing a permanent deal.

All of this set City up to elbow their way into the elite, hampering other clubs in the process, and even spawning that famous "Welcome to Manchester" billboard for Tevez's signing.

Alternate reality: Tevez completes a permanent move to Manchester United in 2009, which stabilizes the club's attack in the wake of Cristiano Ronaldo's world-record £80 million move to Real Madrid the year before. The Argentine continues to dovetail with Wayne Rooney for years, meaning Ferguson's final years at the club are seen out with a bang and two more league titles before he retires in 2013.

Arsenal's barren run ends

Arsenal, meanwhile, avoid the talent drain to City and instead keep Adebayor, Nasri & Co. in north London. It's not enough to convince Robin van Persie to stick around -- he still joins Man United, leading to a short spell where the Dutchman joins Tevez and Rooney in a ferocious attack -- but the Gunners stay strong enough to win a few more domestic cups under Arsène Wenger. As a result, the real-life barren run of zero trophies between 2005 and 2014 never occurs, which means the Frenchman's reign is looked back on even more fondly.

Bale stays at Spurs for a bit longer

On the other side of north London, Tottenham Hotspur -- who narrowly missed out on Champions League football at least three times during City's illicit period -- enjoy something of a golden era. Playing regularly in Europe's top competition allows them to keep Wales winger Gareth Bale a bit longer, who then powers them to a FA Cup win in 2013.

Yes, Real Madrid still sign him for over €100 million, but they have to wait two more years until 2015.

Everton and Aston Villa better off

A chasing pack containing Everton and Aston Villa continually jostle for European spots and occasionally reach the Champions League. Lescott stays and anchors the Toffees' defense for another five seasons, while Barry sees out a long career with Villa, preventing the club from taking the nosedive it actually does.

Newcastle United are still taken over by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) in 2021, but with no City model to follow there isn't the desire to spend much to sign new players and the club continue to fight in midtable rather than challenge for Europe.

Guardiola's career trajectory impacts others

What actually happened: Having cut his teeth in management with Barcelona B in 2007-08, Guardiola took the senior reins at Camp Nou and was responsible for coaching the most aesthetically pleasing style the world had ever seen. It was successful, too: Barça won three LaLiga titles, two Copas del Rey, two Champions Leagues, two Super Cups and two Club World Cups; including all six trophies the club competed for in the calendar year of 2011.

He left in 2012 for a year's sabbatical spent in New York City, before returning to management to take over Bayern Munich in 2013, where seven titles in four years followed.

City's appointment of Guardiola for the 2016-17 season was a landmark moment and backed by a significant cash injection, as well as executives Ferran Soriano and Txiki Begiristain -- who knew him well as a result of decades-long friendships and working relationships at Barcelona -- Guardiola thrived before stepping away this summer.

Guardiola is regarded as one of the greatest-ever influences in the sport and during his 10 years at City, he had a profound effect on several major figures in the game today, which changes a few things for other clubs, too.

Alternate reality: Here, City are nowhere near the level required to persuade Guardiola to join them; they haven't a hope of attracting him to the project and can't spend the kind of money on transfers as he requires. That takes the Spaniard in an entirely different direction after leaving Bayern and he takes another one-year sabbatical.

PSG dominance

Of course, when he returns, Guardiola has his pick of jobs and opts for Paris Saint-Germain, who appoint him instead of Unai Emery in 2016. All the talk is about whether he will reunite with Barcelona legend Lionel Messi in the French capital, but in 2017, Les Parisiens break the world record to sign Barcelona winger Neymar for €222 million, handing Guardiola his superstar difference-maker in attack, while Kylian Mbappé joins for €180 million a year later from Monaco too.

Those two arrivals, combined with Guardiola's tactical nous, is enough to disrupt a period of Champions League dominance that would have otherwise belonged to Real Madrid and Liverpool. Messi never joins, but Guardiola wins two Champions Leagues and helps Neymar to a Ballon d'Or, then abruptly departs in 2020 as he stays true to the pattern displayed in his career to date: Never exceeding four years at one club.

Another sabbatical follows during the COVID-19 pandemic, as Guardiola sees no reason to rush back to the sport while it represents a shell of its usual self.

A dynasty at Arsenal awaits

Then, in 2021, having managed in Spain, Germany and France, and with Italian clubs unable to offer the kind of dominant project he desires, Guardiola makes a much-anticipated move to England.

The top clubs make their pitch. Manchester United's effort is half-hearted, as Solskjaer has just led them to the Premier League title in 2020-21 and they see no major reason to rock the boat; Chelsea are dismissed as too chaotic; Liverpool are building a machine under Klopp. That leaves Arsenal, who have been scratching around for a solution since Wenger departed on good terms in 2018.

It feels a perfect fit: Guardiola's style matches the way the great modern Gunners sides have played. An epic era of success follows, starting with the 2022-23 title and continuing into Europe -- the one title that always eluded Wenger.

Mikel Arteta takes over at PSG

Arteta no longer has his three-year apprenticeship from 2016-19 as Guardiola's assistant coach to give him the grounding he needed before leaping at the chance to be the main man at Arsenal. (He chose that route over a coaching role at Tottenham under Mauricio Pochettino and an offer to manage Arsenal's academy team from Wenger.)

So in this timeline, where Guardiola never joins City and instead takes the PSG job in 2016, Arteta still declines those roles so he can follow Pep to France and learn his craft. When Guardiola departs in 2020, Les Parisiens seek continuity and Arteta sees an opportunity to step up. It takes him time to settle, but he is still there today to battle his former mentor for European supremacy.

Vincent Kompany becomes Mr. Borussia Dortmund

Another of Guardiola's disciples, Kompany, does not come into contact with the Spaniard as a player at City. And rather than become a legend at the Etihad Stadium, he leaves for Borussia Dortmund in 2013, where he and Mats Hummels form a superb central defensive partnership.

Kompany's personality ensures he still ends up in management once he hangs up his boots, but his influences and mentors are different, so he does not go on to espouse Guardiola's style; instead, he coaches a rather more frenetic, Bundesliga-inspired version. He still goes back to Anderlecht to finish his career, but Dortmund come calling again to offer him his first major step into the dugout in 2021.

Luis Enrique back to Barcelona, Enzo Maresca ends up at Tottenham

Luis Enrique -- who in this reality resigns from his post as Spain national team manager after defeat in the Euro 2020 semifinals -- returns to Barcelona in 2021 instead of taking the PSG job.

Enrique hires Maresca (City's current manager, in reality) as his assistant and shows him the secrets of coaching a swashbuckling brand of possession soccer -- instead of Guardiola fine-tuning his possession style. Then, after four long years of study, Tottenham offer Maresca the chance to succeed Ange Postecoglou in 2025 and he takes the leap into management.

Where Man City's star players end up: Silva to Chelsea; Haaland to Arsenal?

What actually happened: Over the past 18 years, City have signed countless stars to power their success to the tune of €3.64 billion. In terms of strikers alone, they moved from Tevez to Agüero to Haaland, with Jesus and Edin Džeko and more sprinkled in between. Every other position more or less followed suit.

Alternate reality: Almost none of those players sign for City. The club is following the financial rules and is simply not in play for them as it isn't successful enough, can't pay enough in fees or wages, and doesn't have Guardiola as manager to tip the scales. This version of City in the transfer window is more akin to Newcastle United; able to make the occasional big signing, but having to let their star names depart regularly in order to balance the books.

Vincent Kompany (2008): He signs for City from Hamburg for around £6 million, but with a lack of silverware and the club's need to break even, the defender moves to Borussia Dortmund in 2013.

Carlos Tevez (2009): Joins Manchester United permanently and continues his dovetailing brilliance with Rooney in attack.

David Silva (2010): Joins Chelsea and flourishes as an attacking midfielder alongside Frank Lampard and Michael Essien.

Yaya Touré (2010): The reported fallout between he and Guardiola at Barcelona still happens, but instead of City, Touré joins his brother Kolo at Arsenal. Finally, the Gunners land their Patrick Vieira replacement in midfield.

Sergio Agüero (2011): Real Madrid crave his signature, but Atlético refuse to do business with their archrivals, so Agüero moves to Juventus instead. Four years and over 100 goals later, Madrid offer the Italian side €80 million and the Old Lady gladly accept, using the money to sign Paulo Dybala from Palermo.

Fernandinho (2015): He still moves to City from Shakhtar Donetsk for £34 million in 2013 but then joins Tottenham as part of the squad rebuilt with the money earned from Bale's mega-transfer to Real Madrid (which happens in 2015 in this reality.)

Raheem Sterling (2015): He continues at Liverpool, happy with the club's 2013-14 Premier League title win and their consistent ability to compete for trophies. He signs a massive new contract at the behest of Rodgers and eventually moves to Chelsea years later.

Kevin De Bruyne (2015): With De Bruyne's reputation hit by his "failure" at Chelsea, City still sign him as their big splash in the market for a club-record £55 million. The difference is he plays only a handful of seasons there, as his brilliance is quickly established and he's scooped up by one of Europe's elite clubs.

John Stones (2016): Chelsea's strong interest lands his signature from Everton; he anchors their defensive line for a decade and replaces John Terry, who retires in 2017.

Aymeric Laporte (2018): The Athletic Bilbao defender signs for Guardiola's Barcelona instead of Clément Lenglet.

Kyle Walker (2017): Joins Chelsea from Spurs and thoroughly enjoys himself as a lung-busting wingback in Antonio Conte's 3-4-3 formation.

Bernardo Silva (2017): Moves to Barcelona just in time to take up Andrés Iniesta's mantle. As a result, the club doesn't spend €40 million to sign Paulinho or €120 million on Philippe Coutinho from Liverpool.

Rodri (2019): Bayern Munich activate the €70 million release clause in his Atletico Madrid contract, allowing them to prepare for life after Thiago Alcântara, who leaves the following year.

Rúben Dias (2020): Manchester United swoop for the Portugal center back because they're struggling to believe in Victor Lindelöf as Harry Maguire's central defensive partner.

Jack Grealish (2021): Also joins Man United, meaning Jadon Sancho doesn't, but his £100 million move is just as unsuccessful as Sancho's was in reality.

Erling Haaland (2022): The whole world competes for the Norway wonderkid's signature as he has a €60 million release clause at Dortmund, but Arsenal win the race as they're able to woo him using a tried-and-trusted question: Would you like to come and play for Guardiola?

Man City are a midtable team

What actually happened: At the time of the Abu Dhabi takeover, City were in dire financial straits. Owner Thaksin Shinawatra was unable to fund the club's day-to-day activities -- let alone make big splashes in the transfer market -- because his assets had been frozen in Thailand due to criminal proceedings being brought against him. It forced City to borrow money to pay costs, which becomes a vicious cycle.

Alternate reality: Given the clubs' long history of bouncing around English football's lower divisions and financial uncertainties, the fans gladly accept stability without a major takeover. Sheikh Mansour still takes over the club to save them from Thaksin, but while there's no mega-spending there's also no financial peril to speak of and zero chance of collapse. The only monetary frustrations the club have are that under the Premier League's Profit and Sustainability (PSR) rules, they can't spend their owner's immeasurable wealth to truly go shoulder-to-shoulder with the big teams.

City float between finishing fifth and 10th in the league, rising and falling depending on fortune, injuries and whatever crisis envelops other clubs. They punch upwards into the Champions League a couple of times and battle well in the cup competitions.

Focus on youth

They're still able to sign very good players -- De Bruyne still joins in 2015, for example -- but don't get to retain him for as long as they'd like. Like Newcastle (and others) in real life, this version of City give in to a big bid and sanction his departure. Still, at least their PSR situation is sorted.

Also helping the PSR situation is a steady flow of youth graduates making it through to the first team squad. OK, their empire doesn't expand to the point where they become a major player in Europe, but the prodigious local talent is still brought through. Defender Micah Richards plays the same integral role after coming through in 2005 and playing for a decade, while winger Shaun Wright-Phillips' second spell at the club is longer, more fruitful and ends with him being labelled a hero.

Other academy prospects who in real life never stood a chance at making the grade, such as Kieran Trippier and Dedryck Boyata, have strong stints at the club. Later down the line, City still produce midfielder Cole Palmer (debut in 2020) and fullback Rico Lewis (2022) -- both born in Greater Manchester -- and the fans get to see plenty more of them. Lewis is a mainstay in a more traditional right back role, while Palmer treats the fans to much more of his talents in attack before moving on.

Managerial merry-go-round

Managerial stability for City is but a dream, and they cycle through options in the dugout just as quickly as every other club in search for a manager who can break their glass ceiling. Robert Martínez is hired off the back of his swashbuckling Wigan Athletic stint; André Villas-Boas is given a third (and final) crack at the Premier League after failing with Chelsea and Tottenham; Alan Pardew acts a stabilizer from 2015-17, before Bournemouth's Eddie Howe is appointed for a long stint and wins the Carabao Cup in 2019, providing a relatively quick success story for his term.

This is a much dimmer reality than the one City actually experienced, where they leapt from title to title, played incredible attacking football, continually signed elite players, and were fortunate enough to be led by one of the greatest managers in history -- but it's one many other law-abiding clubs would long for.

And, in a true reality that could see City relegated in disgrace this season, it's one their fans likely would have embraced back in 2008.

stories.headline: 2026 WNBA Finals feature record African representation as Golden State, Atlanta chase first title
stories.summary: For the first time in WNBA history, the Finals will feature three players and one executive with African connections, the highest African representation in the championship series dating to the league's inaugural season in 1997.
stories.body:
History will be made when the 2026 WNBA Finals between the Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream tips off this Saturday.

For the first time in league history, the Finals will feature three players and one executive with African connections, the highest African representation in the championship series dating to the league's inaugural season in 1997.

Ghanaian-American general manager Ohemaa Nyanin and Canadian forward Laeticia Amihere, whose parents are Ghanaian, represent Golden State, while on the other side, Atlanta have Mali international Sika Kone and Kenyan center Madina Okot.

The four surpass the previous high of three from 2008, when players Olayinka Sanni (Detroit Shock) and Morenike Atunrase (San Antonio Silver Stars) were on opposing teams, with Mike Ekanem serving as strength and conditioning coach for San Antonio.

All three are of Nigerian heritage, and Sanni even represented Nigeria, winning two silver medals and one bronze across three All Africa Games tournaments.

This year's Finals, which begin Saturday in San Francisco, brings together two franchises seeking their first WNBA championship, with Nyanin's leadership of Golden State's basketball operations introducing an executive dimension to Africa's history in the league.

Appointed the Valkyries' inaugural general manager in May 2024, Nyanin became the first executive of African origin in the WNBA, and has overseen one of the fastest rises by an expansion franchise in WNBA history.

Under her leadership, Golden State became the first WNBA expansion team to qualify for the playoffs in their inaugural season in 2025 and followed that by reaching the Finals in only their second season, another expansion franchise record.

The Valkyries finished the 2026 regular season 32-12 before advancing through the playoffs, including a semifinal victory over defending champion Las Vegas Aces.

Nyanin, who previously served as assistant general manager of the New York Liberty team that reached the 2023 Finals, finished third in voting for the WNBA's 2026 Executive of the Year award.

Golden State's success has also been accompanied by record commercial growth. The franchise became the first professional women's sports team to surpass $100 million in annual revenue and topped the WNBA's franchise valuation rankings at about $1 billion, according to May 2026 estimates by CNBC.

The Valkyries also sold out all 44 regular-season home games across their first two seasons, extending their sellout streak through the playoffs.

Although the commercial achievements fall under the wider franchise leadership, Nyanin has been responsible for constructing the roster that has taken Golden State to the championship series in only their second year, a remarkable accomplishment.

Amihere, who was born in Canada to Ghanaian parents, is one member of that roster. The 6-foot-4 forward won the NCAA championship with South Carolina in 2022, helping coach Dawn Staley's Gamecocks defeat Connecticut in the title game. She made history as a teenager in 2017 when, at 15, she became the first Canadian woman to dunk in a competitive game.

The forward was selected eighth overall by Atlanta Dream in the 2023 WNBA draft and has represented Canada at the Olympic Games, including Tokyo in 2021 and Paris in 2024. Her move to Golden State has now brought her to the WNBA Finals for the first time, adding another milestone to a career that has included college and international basketball success.

On the other side of the floor, Atlanta's African representation comes through two players who have followed different routes to the WNBA.

Kone is an established Mali international who developed through one of Africa's most successful women's basketball programs. She was named MVP of the 2021 FIBA Under-19 Women's Basketball World Cup, after leading Mali to a fourth-place finish, the best result by an African team in the tournament's history.

The now 24-year-old averaged 19.7 points and 14.8 rebounds during that competition and was subsequently selected by New York Liberty with the 29th overall pick in the 2022 WNBA draft.

She has also represented Mali at senior level, including at the Women's AfroBasket, where the country has remained one of the leading challengers to Nigeria's continental dominance.

Her appearance on Atlanta's Finals roster continues Mali's history in the championship series. Hamchetou Maiga-Ba won the championship with Sacramento Monarchs in 2005 and returned to the Finals the following year, when Sacramento lost to Detroit Shock.

Okot, meanwhile, has emerged as Kenya's most prominent women's basketball export. The 6-foot-6 center began playing basketball at 16 after initially pursuing volleyball in Kenya, before moving to the United States and establishing herself in college basketball.

She averaged 11.3 points and 9.6 rebounds at Mississippi State during the 2024-25 season before transferring to South Carolina, where she helped the Gamecocks reach the NCAA championship game in 2026. Okot averaged 12.8 points and 10.6 rebounds in her final college season, recording 22 double-doubles.

Atlanta selected her with the 13th overall pick in the 2026 WNBA draft, making her the first Kenyan player selected in the first round, and only the third in league history, following Josephine Owino, a third-round selection in 2009, and Kenyan-American Olivia Nelson-Ododa, who was drafted in the second round in 2022.

Such is the huge influence that Okot has become in Kenya, that the country's President William Ruto came to watch her play in Atlanta's 83-65 victory over New York Liberty in September.

Ruto, who was in New York for the United Nations General Assembly, attended the game with First Lady Rachel Ruto, NBA Deputy Commissioner Mark Tatum and representatives of NBA Africa. Afterward, Ruto and his wife met Okot on the court, took photographs and spoke with her in Swahili.

In her rookie season, she averaged 5.4 points and 3.3 rebounds in 42 regular-season appearances as the Dream returned to the Finals for the first time since 2013.

The presence of the four African-connected figures continues a history dating to the early years of the WNBA. In 2001, just four years after the first Finals, DR Congo's Mwadi Mabika helped the Los Angeles Sparks defeat Charlotte Sting, whose roster included another African, Mozambique's Clarisse Machanguana. Both became the first players of African origin to appear in the Finals.

Mabika returned to the Finals to win a second championship with Los Angeles in 2002, this time against New York Liberty and fellow Congolese player Bernadette Ngoyisa Mudju. But a year later, she was on the other side, as Senegal's Astou Ndiaye-Diatta won the championship with Detroit Shock, defeating Mabika and the Sparks.

Those three consecutive Finals established an early precedent for African-born players appearing on opposing teams in the championship series. In total, players of African origin have been in 15 of the league's 29 previous Finals, with 16 distinct players and 22 total player appearances.

Nigeria, as expected, have had more players in WNBA Finals roster than any other African country, with five including Sanni, Natalia Achonwa, Ogwumike, Liz Cambage and Ezi Magbegor.

Los Angeles have also won more championships with African-connected players than any other franchise, claiming three through Mabika's two titles and Nigerian-American forward Ogwumike's championship in 2016.

Ogwumike, who won the league's MVP award that season, scored the decisive basket in Game 5 against Minnesota Lynx and returned to the Finals in 2017, but was second time unlucky when Los Angeles lost the title to Minnesota.

Mabika remains the most successful African-born player in league history, with two titles from three Finals appearances. Eight players of African origin have been WNBA champions, for a total of nine titles.

These include Seattle Storm's Magbegor, whose family has Nigerian roots, in 2020; Senegal-born Astou Ndour-Fall with Chicago Sky in 2021; and Nyara Sabally, whose father is Gambian, with New York Liberty in 2024, along with Hamchetou Maiga-Ba, and Olayinka Sanni.

The African connection also extended beyond the playing roster. Ekanem's involvement with San Antonio in 2008 helped establish the previous high for African representation in a Finals series, while Nigerian origin athletic trainer Michelle Anumba was part of the Las Vegas Aces' back-to-back championship teams in 2022 and 2023.

This year's championship series adds the front office into that history, with Nyanin overseeing the basketball operations of a Golden State team attempting to win a title in only their second season.

Atlanta, who have lost three previous Finals appearances in 2010, 2011 and 2013, are hoping to heal from the trauma of those losses by putting the memory behind them to claim their first championship in franchise history.

The series opens on Saturday at Chase Center, with one franchise guaranteed to win its first WNBA title. But more importantly for Africa, whichever team wins that first chip, there will be at least two Africans on the podium when that final buzzer goes.

stories.headline: F1 2027 driver lineups: Who has a seat - and who's out of contract?
stories.summary: The 2026 rule changes threw Formula 1 into a new era of challenges and uncertainty, but the real moments of unpredictability are still to come.
stories.body:
The 2026 rule changes threw Formula 1 into a new era of challenges and uncertainty, but the real moments of unpredictability are still to come.

Most drivers secured short-term deals to survive the regulation shift, leaving the grid wide open for the following year. With only a handful of drivers locked into long-term contracts almost every seat on the grid is up for grabs.

Here is our early look at what the future holds for the current Formula 1 lineup.

McLaren

Lando Norris - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2030

Prior to the start of the 2024 F1 season Norris agreed to an "extended multi-year contract beyond 2025."

The reigning champion has now signed a new contract with McLaren until at least 2030. The deal, which includes one of his title-winning Formula 1 cars as a gift from the team, also has the option of a "multi-year" extension beyond 2030.

Oscar Piastri - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2026

Ahead of the first race of the 2025 F1 season Piastri also signed a multi-year contract extension. His previous deal already ran until the end of 2026, and his latest agreement is likely to keep him at McLaren until at least the end of 2028 -- though speculation continues to rumble on about his long-term future.

Ferrari

Lewis Hamilton - 2027

While an exact end date of Hamilton's contract -- signed after completing one of the biggest driver moves in F1 history -- was never officially communicated, Hamilton admitted earlier this year that he still had a contract in place for 2027. That means he got at least a three-year deal at Ferrari, something he had also been seeking at Mercedes.

Amid retirement rumours, Hamilton has also crushed speculation and assured fans that he wasn't going anywhere just yet.

He said: "There's a lot of people that are trying to retire me, and that's not even in my thoughts. I'm already thinking of what will be next, and planning for, like, the next five years. But I still plan to be here for some time."

Charles Leclerc - 2028

Leclerc, who first joined Ferrari in 2019, signed another multi-year extension ahead of the 2026 Monaco Grand Prix.

The team did not publicly reveal an exact expiry date, but the new agreement is understood to take Leclerc to 2028 and potentially beyond, giving Ferrari long-term security over one side of its driver lineup.

Red Bull

Max Verstappen - 2030

Red Bull confirmed in 2022 that four-time world champion Verstappen would remain with the team until the end of 2028 in one of the longest deals on the F1 grid.

Sources told ESPN that performance-related clauses in Verstappen's contract could allow him to leave early, but the Dutchman has now signed a new contract extension with Red Bull until 2030 ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix.

Isack Hadjar - 2027

Isack Hadjar was promoted from Racing Bulls to partner Verstappen for the 2026 season after an impressive rookie campaign. He has now signed a contract extension with Red Bull, securing his seat for the 2027 season.

Mercedes

George Russell - beyond 2026

Russell agreed a new deal with Mercedes ahead of the 2026 season following lengthy negotiations with team principal Toto Wolff.

Although the agreement was initially confirmed as taking him through at least 2026, Russell has since described it as a multi-year deal and said he will fulfill the performance clauses in his contract to stay at Mercedes next year.

Kimi Antonelli - TBC

Mercedes' Antonelli has only been given one-year contracts since his debut, but given his form this season there's no way he'll be leaving the Silver Arrows. Right?

No official announcements have been made yet, but Antonelli could be celebrating both a maiden title and a bumper new deal this year.

Aston Martin

Fernando Alonso - TBC

Alonso's current Aston Martin deal runs until the end of the 2026 season, and he said a decision on his future will come later in the year. At 45 years old, the decision is likely to be between continuing with an underperforming Aston Martin team, or calling time on his F1 career once and for all.

Lance Stroll - TBC

Stroll signed a contract extension in 2024 which kept him with Aston Martin for 2025 "and beyond," but no specific end date was announced. Part of that ambiguity, of course, is because he's the son of team owner Lawrence Stroll.

He remains with the team for 2026, although his position for 2027 has not formally been confirmed.

Alpine

Pierre Gasly - 2028

Gasly is one of the drivers whose future is already settled -- the Frenchman signed a new multi-year agreement with Alpine in 2025 which keeps him locked in at the team until at least the end of the 2028 season.

Franco Colapinto - 2027

Colapinto retained his Alpine seat alongside Gasly for 2026 after taking over from Jack Doohan during the previous season. He has now signed a new contract with the team, meaning the Argentinian will continue with Alpine for the 2027 season.

Haas

Rafael Câmara - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2027

F2 star Câmara will replace Esteban Ocon for the 2027 season on a multi-year agreement. The reigning Formula 3 champion and current Formula 2 leader will make his debut in F1 and will partner fellow Ferrari Driver Academy member Oliver Bearman.

Oliver Bearman - TBC

Bearman joined Haas on a multi-year deal when he became a full-time F1 driver in 2025. The exact duration of Bearman's contract has not been made public, leaving his 2027 status uncertain for now.

However, sources with good knowledge of the team's thinking have told ESPN that Bearman is almost certain to stay with the team in 2027 unless a Ferrari seat opens up, then the Englishman remains effectively loaned to Haas.

Racing Bulls

Liam Lawson - TBC

Lawson remained with Racing Bulls for 2026 after rebuilding his season following a short-lived promotion to Red Bull the previous year.

His seat is only confirmed for the current season, meaning the New Zealander will again have to prove his case if he is to stay within the Red Bull set-up in 2027.

Arvid Lindblad - TBC

Lindblad became the latest Red Bull junior to make the jump to Formula 1 when he was handed a Racing Bulls seat for 2026.

The rookie is currently only confirmed for this season and the team have played down speculation over their driver lineup for 2027. You'd be shocked to see him go anywhere, though.

Williams

Carlos Sainz - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2026

Sainz originally joined Williams on a deal covering the 2025 and 2026 seasons, with "options to extend" his stay beyond that. He has recently spoken about wanting to make the Williams project work, leading to him signing a new multi-year extension with the team.

Alex Albon - 2027

Albon signed a new one-year contract with Williams during the summer break, tying him down for the 2027 season. The short-term deal is interesting, given Albon's last contract -- signed in 2024 -- was for multiple years. Keeping those options open?

Audi

Nico Hulkenberg - TBC

Hulkenberg joined Sauber ahead of its transformation into the Audi team on a multi-year contract in 2025.

There are believed to be options in his deal which could allow him to remain with Audi beyond 2026, but an exact end date has not been announced.

Gabriel Bortoleto - TBC

Bortoleto joined Hulkenberg at Sauber before the team's transition to Audi and also signed a multi-year deal.

The Brazilian is contracted through at least the end of 2026, but his place for 2027 has not yet been officially confirmed.

Cadillac

Sergio Perez - 2027

Perez returned to the Formula 1 grid with Cadillac for the team's debut season in 2026 after spending a year away from racing.

The Mexican joined on a multi-year agreement understood to be on similar terms to teammate Valtteri Bottas, putting him in line to remain with Cadillac for 2027.

Valtteri Bottas - 2027

Bottas also returned to a full-time race seat with Cadillac after spending 2025 as Mercedes' reserve driver.

The Finn signed a multi-year deal which runs until at least the end of 2027, giving the new team one of the few already settled driver pairings heading into next season.

stories.headline: Shakhtar's Champions League win vs. AEK was more than just a game
stories.summary: Shakhtar Donetsk haven't played at home since 2014 due to the war, and this season, their Champions League home games are at Chelsea's Stamford Bridge. Wednesday's win was a reminder of how absurd their situation is.
stories.body:
LONDON -- Take a step back and revel in the absurdity for a minute. Shakhtar Donetsk, a Ukrainian team from the Russian-speaking part of the country, are playing a Greek team, AEK Athens, in London, at Chelsea's Stamford Bridge. Technically, it's a "home game," but that concept has become rather meaningless.

Shakhtar haven't played at their home, the Donbas Arena, since May 2014, some 650 weeks ago. They turn up wherever someone will host them: Odessa, Kyiv, Kharkiv and Lviv for Ukrainian league games; Warsaw, Hamburg, Gelsenkirchen, Krakow, Ljubljana and now London for matches in European competition. Why? Because their opponents can't (or won't) travel to Ukraine, where none of the civilian airports are open, air raid sirens go off a dozen times a day, and where drones and bombs can't be trusted to distinguish between a military captain and the captain of a soccer team.

It's pretty obvious that in those circumstances, you're more than a club -- you're a symbol of defiance, an attempt to maintain some sort of normality in the face of a war that has taken more than half a million lives and displaced tens of millions more.

"We are playing for people from Ukraine all over the world," sporting director Dario Srna said. "Everywhere we've gone, they've come [to see us]. We represent Ukraine in the center of the world: we're not just playing for us. [We are] a Ukrainian team, we are not just Shakhtar."

But, of course, nothing is normal. Everything is messed up, and their mere presence in the Champions League constitutes a political dimension.

Wednesday night, Shakhtar were at Stamford Bridge, the home of Chelsea. Resourceful as ever, street vendors outside the ground hawked their off-brand scarves, except rather than "Cole Palmer," "João Pedro" and "John Terry," the names read "Pedrinho," "[Mykola] Matviyenko" and "[Valeriy] Bondar." Watching over them was a life-size cardboard cutout of Dwayne Johnson, aka The Rock, only his face was replaced by that of Ukrainian President Vladimir Zelenskyy.

Inside, visiting AEK fans -- who turned the Shed End into a two-tier wall of tifo, flags and noise -- outsing, if not outnumber, the "home" support.

Because yes, this is Shakhtar's home for the Champions League this season, a move made possible by the London club's failure to qualify for European competitions (and, probably, a need to rake in some extra rent on those empty weeknights). Ironically, Chelsea's previous owner, Roman Abramovich, was forced by the U.K. government to sell the club after the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, because of his ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Abramovich holds passports from Portugal, Israel and Russia. His yachts are moored in Turkey.

Abramovich, whose mother is Ukrainian, is a complicated figure. So is Shakhtar's version of Abramovich, Rinat Akhmetov.

An ethnic Russian, but Donetsk-born and bred, Akhmetov's huge wealth from mining and energy bankrolled the club's rise to prominence prewar -- lest we forget, the likes of Willian and Fernandinho, Henrikh Mkiytaryan and Douglas Costa are all Shakhtar alums -- and keeps it alive and very much kicking today. Forbes estimates his wealth at nearly $8 billion and like most folks of that ilk, Akhmetov could easily have made different choices, decamping abroad. When the war broke out, he chose to stay, and that was not something to take for granted, given that he had previously clashed with Zelenskyy and, in the 2000s, served in parliament in the party of former pro-Russian Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych, whom he also backed financially.

Akhmetov broke with Yanukovych in 2014 and while his pro-Ukrainian words today are loud, his actions -- from staying in the country to tirelessly campaigning to his efforts with Shakhtar -- speak even louder.

"He can't leave Ukraine, not after seeing what he has seen," Srna says of Akhmetov. "It's impossible. He's devoted himself to this, helping the economy, helping the people. All while sleeping each night under bombs."

Many Ukrainians have no choice, which makes the actions of those who could be elsewhere all the more remarkable. It takes an unconventional type of person.

Most of Shakhtar's players are Brazilian -- lured by money, sure, but also the opportunity to showcase their talent. The coach, former Atletico Madrid and Barcelona standout Arda Turan, is Turkish. Even if you don't remember what he was like as a player, watching him prowl the technical area during the AEK game, fists clenched and eyes wild, you come to understand how this is the same guy who once got into an altercation with a pop star in an Istanbul hospital, a brawl that ended in him firing a gun into the floor.

Srna himself is Croatian, but has been at the club -- first as a player then as sporting director -- for 23 years. He too could have left umpteen times and, in fact, he says he even turned down the chance to take over Barcelona's recruitment a decade ago.

"Ukraine and Shakhtar are in my blood," he says. "If I leave now, I couldn't live with myself."

In some ways, Srna has been here before. He was eight years old when civil war broke out in the former Yugoslavia in March 1991. The conflict that would rage for 4½ years, ripped apart communities along ethnic lines. Neighbors took up arms against neighbors. His own father woke up every day supplying baked goods for the military. If you've seen the ESPN 30 for 30 documentary "Once Brothers" about the relationship between Drazen Petrovic and Vlade Divac, well ... he lived it. Twice. Maybe that's why he soldiers on, numb to what he is experiencing.

"I have this feeling inside myself," he says. "It's a feeling I felt before [as a child experiencing war in Croatia]. But when you feel that pain and it comes back to you again, well, you're not going to have the same pain twice. I know this pain. I know this feeling ..."

Srna trails off as he searches for the right words of history -- the worst parts -- repeating itself with him in the middle of it. But then he flickers back with righteous anger.

"This is unbelievable, I can't explain it," he says. "Four-and-a-half years [this war has continued]. Bombing each other, destroying everything ... for what? For f---ing what? People die, families are destroyed, children are traumatized and grow up with psychological problems ..."

On this Wednesday night, even as Shakhtar emerge as 3-1 victors over AEK, you're reminded once again of the difficulties. The team were up at 6 a.m. on Thursday to catch a 10 o'clock flight on a plane they chartered from a budget airline taking them back to Rzeszow in Poland. They'll then board a bus back across the border into Ukraine, arriving -- best-case scenario -- at 9 p.m. local time. All this not knowing whether they'll have power and heat when they arrive, or whether they'll be making regular trips into the air raid shelter.

You want to end on a note of hope. Srna does his best to offer it, but he clearly isn't going to lie to you or to himself.

"We [Croatians] have more or less an OK relationship now with Serbia," he says. "Time [30 years have passed] is helping, generations change, it's different people. We take a step back and understand what was good, what was not good. We can't say all Serbian people are bad ... But in this moment, it's not possible to be friends with a Russian person. In time, maybe a few years, maybe many years, I don't know ... right now though, it's impossible."

Certainly more impossible than a club without a home in a country at war defying logic and competing in the Champions League against the likes of Real Madrid, who visit Stamford Bridge on Jan. 27.

One of the side effects of war is the normalization of the horrific and the absurd. Shakhtar's plight has, by necessity, normalized the absurd, in an effort to stave off the horrific.

stories.headline: UFC champ Alexander Volkanovski proposes 'send-off' superbout vs. Justin Gaethje
stories.summary: UFC featherweight champion Alexander Volkanovski is calling for a "send-off" superfight against lightweight champion Justin Gaethje.
stories.body:
UFC featherweight champion Alexander Volkanovski has proposed a "send-off" superfight between himself and lightweight champion Justin Gaethje.

Volkanovski (28-4) is scheduled to defend his 145-pound title against Movsar Evloev (20-0) at UFC 333 on Oct. 24 in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. Arguably the greatest featherweight of all time, Volkanovski has acknowledged he is approaching the end of his career at 38 years old. Gaethje, 37, has acknowledged the same since he claimed the UFC's 155-pound title for the first time in June.

With both champions seemingly near the end of their time in the Octagon, Volkanovski has suggested a winner-take-all scenario in 2027.

"Imagine that, do it as a send-off," Volkanovski told the "Who Da Fook Are These Guys?" podcast. "Gaethje, Volk. I think he's said that he maybe has one more. That could be a superfight. Let's do a superfight with the lightweight title on the line. We can both see everyone off with a crazy superfight. That could be really good."

Volkanovski, of Australia, has already tried to capture the lightweight title. He famously challenged then-lightweight champion Islam Makhachev twice in a 10-month span in 2023. He suffered a razor-close decision loss to Makhachev in their first meeting in February then lost by first-round knockout in an October rematch that was scheduled on short notice.

Gaethje (28-5) has not even guaranteed whether he will fight again or retire off his historic win at the White House in June, but he has stated that he believes his next challenger would be lightweight contender Arman Tsarukyan. Volkanovski appears to be throwing his name into the mix in the hope of changing those plans.

"He's said, 'What's the point of doing rematches,'" Volkanovski said. "Let's do a superfight then [retire] straight away after, let the divisions sort themselves out. The UFC would be happy for that. Let's make it happen."

stories.headline: Judge sides with NRL over NZ Rugby on Chiefs name
stories.summary: Rugby league has struck the first blow in the Chief name wars, with New Zealand Rugby's urgent injunction denied ahead of the new PNG NRL club's jersey reveal.
stories.body:
New Zealand's High Court has knocked back an application for an interim injunction on the PNG Chiefs NRL franchise using its name in the country.

New Zealand Rugby (NZR) had rushed to court ahead of the PNG team's logo and jersey reveal in Port Moresby next week.

The organisation claimed use of the Chiefs name, also the name of the long-standing Super Rugby Pacific outfit, would cause confusion and damage to the brand value.

But a judge at Friday's two-hour Wellington hearing turned down the application after hearing an injunction could harm the NRL expansion outfit's efforts to attract players ahead of a 2028 debut.

The dispute remains though, with the application for a final injunction still before the court and legal action in Australia a consideration.

ARLC executive chairman Peter V'landys last week labelled NZR's action one of "mind-blowing hypocrisy", using the example of the Auckland Blues' arrival decades after the NSW Blues "had been the Blues".

"Today's decision is not a judgement on the strength of our case, and the matter will still be heard in full," NZR boss Steve Lancaster said.

"As the trademark holder, our responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand hasn't changed. We remain open to working with the ARLC on a solution."

NZR's lawyer Earl Gray argued on Friday that the PNG Chiefs' use of 'PNG Chiefs' and 'Chiefs' interchangeably created confusion for fans of both codes and that, with no clear distinction between the two, it would strip the rugby Chiefs' brand exclusivity.

He said NZR had trademark protections for the Chiefs in New Zealand that the NRL had not acknowledged.

ARLC laywer Clive Elliot argued that the request for an urgent injunction, about a year after NZR became aware of the PNG Chiefs name, was not appropriate.

He said an injunction now would cloud the franchise's reputation ahead of a recruitment blitz once free agency opens in November.
